opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's important to be honest about that. Single Deep CFR was a small, incremental contribution. I was still a teenager, working mostly on my own, and I was standing entirely on the shoulders of people like Noam and Tuomas Sandholm and the broader CFR community. Deep CFR had already shown that you could replace the big tabular regret tables with neural networks, and my contribution was essentially noticing that you could simplify it. Instead of training a separate average-strategy network, you could store the value networks from each iteration and sample from them, which removed a source of approximation error and made the algorithm cleaner and, in some settings, a bit better.

So it was a nice idea, and it got me in the door, but it's not in the same category as what Noam did. Libratus and Pluribus were genuine breakthroughs. They beat top professionals at no-limit hold'em, including six-player games, which a lot of people thought was years away. That required combining search, abstraction, and real engineering at a scale and level of rigor that's very different from tweaking an algorithm on small benchmark games.

What I'd say the work meant for me personally is that it taught me how research actually works. You read everything, find a seam where something can be simpler or more principled, and then do the experiments carefully. And it got me talking to people like Noam, which was enormously valuable. But in the grand scheme of the field it was a footnote, and I'm fine with that. I'm much more excited about what I've been working on since.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd put it in perspective by saying it was a footnote to his work, and I mean that in the most flattering way possible for Noam.

The context is that I was a teenager, basically self-taught, and I was obsessed with poker AI because it was the clearest example of a game where you had to reason about hidden information. Noam and Tuomas Sandholm had just done Libratus, and the whole field was built on counterfactual regret minimization, this iterative algorithm that converges to a Nash equilibrium. The problem was that CFR in its pure form needs to touch the whole game tree, which is absurd for anything the size of no-limit hold'em. So everyone was using abstraction, bucketing hands together, and that's where a lot of the art was.

Then Noam published Deep CFR, which was the first time someone really showed you could replace the giant tables with a neural network and have it actually work. That was the real breakthrough. What I did with Single Deep CFR was a simplification of that. Deep CFR trained two kinds of networks, one for the regrets and one for the average strategy, and the second one was awkward, you had to store a huge buffer of past strategies and fit a network to it. I noticed you could just skip that entirely and sample from the regret networks of past iterations to get the average policy for free. It was cleaner, it had one less thing to go wrong, and in my experiments it did a bit better.

So the way I think about it is: Noam opened the door and showed there was a room there. I walked in and moved a piece of furniture. That's genuinely how I'd describe it. It was a nice idea, it got me noticed, it's the reason I ended up talking to people at DeepMind and later Facebook AI, but it wasn't the kind of thing that changes what's possible. Deep CFR, and then ReBeL after it, those changed what was possible.

And I think that distinction mattered a lot for me personally. There's a temptation when you're young and you get a paper that people cite to think you're a peer of the people whose shoulders you're standing on. I was lucky in that I got to actually work with Noam afterward, and when you're in the room with someone who really sees the whole problem, you learn very quickly what the gap is between a contribution and an insight. That was probably more valuable than the paper itself.

astra-6.text: I’d put it in perspective as a fairly narrow contribution. Noam’s research laid a lot of the groundwork, including Deep Counterfactual Regret Minimization. My Single Deep CFR work built directly on that and showed a way to simplify part of the approach while improving performance in the settings I tested. I was proud of that result, but it’s very different from the breadth of research and engineering behind something like superhuman poker. I wouldn’t frame it as me having surpassed Noam—it was a useful contribution on top of foundational work he and others had done.

I wouldn’t equate it with the broader body of work Noam had done on poker and imperfect-information games.
